title: No more pyramids: Rethinking your workforce for the agentic AI era
author: Shebani Patel · Brad Herndon · Danielle Phaneuf · Bob Woods

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Staffing structure: AI threatens both pyramid and pipeline
st.an: PwC accepts that agentic AI disrupts the pyramid by automating entry-level tasks and reducing routine management, then materially develops the cluster’s proposition with a specific hourglass model for knowledge-intensive firms. It argues for preserving junior apprenticeship to sustain future expertise and AI oversight, while redesigning roles, workflows, career paths and accountability together rather than treating staffing shape as an isolated choice.
qs: If you don’t build your pipeline now, you may soon find yourself without the expertise and leadership needed to correct AI-generated errors, spot systemic risk, or seize new market opportunities.

- **Map out the impact.** As you construct or assess an AI business case, make sure that it covers which roles are likely to be automated, augmented, or created—and what these changes mean for headcount, career paths, and reskilling.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: PwC accepts the cluster’s core work-redesign thesis and extends it with concrete finance and IT operating-model examples: agents absorb routine and multi-step execution while professionals shift toward judgment, strategy and business outcomes. It also specifies corresponding changes to skills, roles and organisational structure. However, these are directional predictions outside legal practice, not empirical evidence about legal AI’s jagged capabilities or verification constraints.
qs: Here’s what CFOs and finance leaders should know:  - Shift from number-crunching to business value.** As AI agents execute routine tasks, people can apply financial judgment and commercial awareness to translate agent-produced analyses into performance drivers, tradeoffs, and strategic implications—helping the business make better decisions.
But realizing this opportunity depends on making intentional changes to focus, roles, and structure.

st.t: Work redesign: Organisation captures more value than access
st.an: The source accepts that AI value depends on organisational redesign rather than tool access alone and materially develops the proposition with an implementation framework: redesign workflows around AI, explicitly allocate work among AI and people, preserve human accountability, and incorporate headcount, reskilling and career-path effects into the business case.
qs: - **Redesign workflows—and think big.** Instead of asking how AI can improve a process, ask how you can reinvent it with AI at the core.
- **Clarify who does what.** For each role in an AI-enabled workflow, classify the work into AI-only / human + AI / human-only, then rewrite role purpose and skills accordingly.

kp.k: Agent orchestration can turn specialists into outcome-focused generalists
kp.d: PwC argues that agents performing multistep, high-skill tasks can broaden experienced specialists’ responsibilities across workflows. It describes this shift as already underway across industries, back offices and frontline teams, while conditioning increased worker value on appropriate skills and role design. Its software-development example illustrates the proposed mechanism rather than reporting a measured productivity result.
qs: One experienced software engineer can orchestrate teams of AI agents at work in many or even all stages.

As they shift from narrow execution to broader responsibility, these engineers—and other specialized, high-value employees like them—can become generalists: working across more processes, making faster decisions, and focusing on bottom-line impact.

kp.k: Apprenticeship preserves expertise needed to oversee AI
kp.d: PwC argues that AI-enabled generalists depend on a pipeline combining AI literacy with specialized, real-world apprenticeship. Prior experience doing work without agents supplies the expertise to recognize errors and systemic risks. It warns that neglecting early-career development could undermine future expertise and leadership, rather than presenting such depletion as an established outcome.
qs: The new generalists don’t build themselves.
That software engineer can work over the full development cycle because they’ve already built software without AI agents’ help.
If you don’t build your pipeline now, you may soon find yourself without the expertise and leadership needed to correct AI-generated errors, spot systemic risk, or seize new market opportunities.

kp.k: AI may accelerate early-career contribution without eliminating training
kp.d: PwC presents faster meaningful contribution by agent-equipped early-career workers as a likely benefit. As an internal accounting example, it reports that its audit teams use AI for specialized tasks and that entry-level training now includes agent use, critical thinking, independence, audit quality, data security and clients’ broader needs. No quantified training or performance outcomes accompany this example.
qs: At PwC, for example, our audit teams use AI to help execute many specialized audit tasks and deliver a more seamless client experience.
and to think critically, support our longstanding focus on independence, audit quality, and data security, and focus on clients’ big-picture needs.

kp.k: Diamond structures risk weakening the future talent pipeline
kp.d: PwC describes some companies reducing entry-level staffing as agents assume data gathering, processing and reporting, while repurposing the middle tier to train and oversee agents. The resulting diamond may improve agility and agent management at scale, but PwC cautions against adopting it by default: knowledge-intensive businesses could sacrifice apprenticeship and future leaders with organization-specific experience. These are organizational staffing shapes, not legal-firm leverage measurements.
qs: The result is a diamond-shaped structure: a small leadership team, a strong middle layer, and a narrow base of new talent.
But it should be a choice, not a default, because for many companies, this diamond structure can carry medium- and long-term risks.
If your company is based on knowledge work, reducing early-career workers could limit apprenticeship and starve your organization of its future:

kp.k: PwC favors an hourglass for knowledge-intensive organizations
kp.d: PwC says it is building an hourglass structure internally and proposes it as a potentially better choice for knowledge-intensive firms. A capable early-career base develops rapidly with AI, specialists extend their reach, and a leaner middle connects workers to leadership. Reduced routine supervision is expected to lower demand for middle managers, while experienced workers move into exception handling, coaching and consequential decisions rather than simply disappearing.
qs: For these knowledge-intensive firms, an hourglass structure—which we’re building in-house at PwC—can be a better choice.
Instead, these experienced workers can take on higher-skill roles in exception handling, coaching, and high-value decision-making.
With a strong, capable base and a forward-looking leadership tier, connected by a lean, high-performing middle, your org chart looks like an hourglass.

kp.k: Finance roles broaden while location and skill requirements shift
kp.d: PwC describes finance professionals directing specialized agents across modeling, risk and compliance, and accounts payable and receivable. It anticipates greater speed and capacity, declining offshore roles, consolidated onshore roles and new strategy-oriented positions. Finance fundamentals remain necessary, supplemented by AI, analytics, commercial judgment and business collaboration; the proposed operating model makes finance a growth contributor rather than only a back-office function.
qs: Offshore roles begin to decline, while onshore roles consolidate and shift.
New positions emerge, focused on strategy, insight, and business outcomes.
People with strong skills in finance fundamentals remain vital.

kp.k: IT moves toward workflow design and AI oversight
kp.d: PwC predicts that agents handling support and quality-assurance tasks may reduce maintenance and troubleshooting resource requirements. With deliberate changes to roles and structure, IT could shift from responding to business needs toward shaping intelligent workflows and innovation. Proposed responsibilities include agent orchestration, model oversight, business integration and workflow design.
qs: With AI agents handling many support and QA tasks, fewer resources may be needed for maintenance and troubleshooting.
Existing roles can evolve to include model oversight, business integration, and workflow design—helping to turn more IT professionals into high-impact contributors.

kp.k: Marketing generalists may consolidate workflows and senior roles
kp.d: PwC argues that agent execution across content, campaigns, planning and analytics can enable marketers to manage the full cycle while emphasizing creativity, strategy and customer connection. It also suggests that a smaller group of senior leaders could absorb formerly distinct leadership responsibilities. These are proposed organizational possibilities, not quantified staffing or effectiveness findings.
qs: As agents take on more specialized work, marketers can manage the full cycle—from planning through activation and analysis

With specialized AI agents at their command, a small group of senior leaders who understand the customer, drive demand, and grow customer lifetime value could take on many distinct, senior roles that currently cover marketing strategy, planning, customer experience, digital, paid media, analytics, and more.

kp.k: HR automation could redirect effort toward workforce strategy
kp.d: PwC proposes HR generalists directing agents for routine work while HR business partners concentrate on business outcomes and team-based development. It says an AI-enabled operating model can reduce human effort by 40% to 50% across HR, freeing capacity for incentives, succession, location and workforce planning. The figure links to another PwC article; this document supplies no underlying sample, measurement method or study period.
qs: They can, for example, create bespoke, x-capability focused pods and upskill these pods not by position, but as a team.
With a new, AI-enabled HR operating model, you can reduce human effort by [40% to 50% across HR](/us/en/tech-effect/ai-analytics/agentic-ai-in-hr.html).

kp.k: Workflow redesign retains human authority and outcome accountability
kp.d: PwC recommends leadership-led investment in high-impact areas and fundamental workflow reinvention rather than incremental process improvement. It presents a potential reduction of as much as 50% in human effort, not an observed general result or an equivalent headcount reduction. Despite task automation, its recommended model keeps people responsible for major decisions and outcomes.
qs: Leadership identifies a few high-impact areas for investment, sets a clear strategy, and guides a focused path to value.
Instead of asking how AI can improve a process, ask how you can reinvent it with AI at the core.
People should be at the helm: always in charge, always making the big decisions, and always accountable for outcomes.
But AI agents may be able to shave off as much as 50% of human effort.

kp.k: Workforce planning should explicitly allocate human and AI work
kp.d: PwC recommends assessing which roles will be automated, augmented or created and the implications for headcount, career paths and reskilling. Organizations should classify work by human and AI participation, rewrite role purposes and skills, and create explicit AI collaboration profiles for critical positions. It also recommends modernized job catalogs, common AI responsibilities and skills, and sustained recruitment and development of early-career talent.
qs: As you construct or assess an AI business case, make sure that it covers which roles are likely to be automated, augmented, or created—and what these changes mean for headcount, career paths, and reskilling.
For each role in an AI-enabled workflow, classify the work into AI-only / human + AI / human-only, then rewrite role purpose and skills accordingly.
For critical roles, create an explicit “AI collaboration profile” that defines how AI should be used, what should remain human, and which skills matter most.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: PwC’s authors predict broader AI-enabled generalist roles, redesigned staffing structures and reduced human effort across business functions, while arguing for preservation of early-career talent pipelines.
pts.d: Shebani Patel, Brad Herndon, Danielle Phaneuf and Bob Woods make cross-domain claims about enterprise work, not specific claims about legal services. They argue that agents performing multistep, high-skill tasks allow experienced specialists to take responsibility across workflows: one software engineer, for example, can orchestrate agents across many or all development stages. AI-equipped early-career employees can contribute sooner, but apprenticeship remains necessary to develop expertise for correcting AI errors, identifying systemic risk and leading the business. The authors describe some companies narrowing their entry-level base and retaining a strong middle layer to oversee agents, producing a diamond structure. They say this can improve operations but risks weakening future expertise in knowledge-intensive firms. For those firms, they propose an hourglass with a strong entry-level base, expanded specialist reach and a leaner middle; routine management declines while experienced workers move toward exception handling, coaching and consequential decisions. In finance, they anticipate declining offshore roles, consolidated onshore roles and new strategy-oriented positions. In IT, fewer resources may be needed for support and maintenance, with roles shifting toward agent orchestration, model oversight and workflow design. In marketing, generalists can manage the full cycle and a smaller senior group could absorb previously distinct leadership roles. In HR, agents can reduce human effort by 40% to 50%, freeing capacity for strategic workforce work. More generally, redesigned workflows may reduce human effort by as much as 50%. These are effort-reduction claims, not equivalent quantified predictions of job losses.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is primarily the authors’ professional observations, PwC’s own practices and links to related publications; the supplied text does not report a measured evaluation of the predicted gains.
pts.d: The authors describe generalist roles and agentic workflows as developments they are already observing across industries and functions. Their concrete organizational examples are PwC’s audit teams using AI for specialized tasks, training entry-level auditors in agent use and critical thinking, and PwC building an hourglass structure internally. The software engineer example illustrates a capability claim rather than presenting a documented comparative case. The article links to PwC’s 2026 AI Business Predictions, function-specific operating-model articles and an external account of PwC training. The 40%–50% HR effort-reduction claim links to another PwC article, but the supplied document gives no underlying sample, method, baseline or measured results. The broader claim of up to 50% less human effort likewise has no accompanying calculation or benchmark in this text. These bases should be recorded as practitioner observation, organizational experience and linked authority rather than as independently demonstrated productivity or employment outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article presents the shift as already underway in 2026, with conditional future gains and medium- to long-term risks, but no dated completion forecast.
pts.d: The authors describe current agent capabilities and emerging role changes while urging leaders to act now. Faster early-career contribution is qualified as a likely benefit when workers are equipped with agents. Broader specialist responsibilities depend on appropriate skills, role design and accumulated experience, including experience gained without agent assistance. Transformation requires deliberate workflow redesign, team restructuring, training and leadership investment rather than simply adding technology. Diamond structures can suit some businesses, but narrowing the entry-level base may harm knowledge-intensive organizations over the medium and long term. Hourglass structures are presented as a potentially better choice for those firms, not a universal outcome. Functional changes are explicitly nonuniform. The model combines automation of selected tasks with human direction and accountability rather than unrestricted substitution: work should be divided into AI-only, human-plus-AI and human-only categories. The percentage effort reductions are possibilities under redesigned AI-enabled operating models, not guaranteed results or timed headcount forecasts.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are enterprise leaders, experienced specialists, junior workers, middle managers and staff across finance, IT, marketing, HR and audit.
pts.d: CEOs, CFOs, CIOs and CHROs are asked to redesign roles, staffing and talent development; the marketing discussion also addresses CMOs. Experienced specialists gain broader workflow ownership and agent-supervision responsibilities. Early-career workers face contrasting possibilities: reduced hiring in diamond structures or expanded, faster-contributing roles in hourglass structures. Knowledge-intensive organizations risk losing their future expert and leadership pipeline if they cut junior roles. Middle managers face reduced demand for routine supervision and potential movement into coaching, exception handling and high-value decisions. Finance changes affect offshore and onshore workers differently; IT support and QA work may require fewer resources; marketing specialists and senior leaders may see responsibilities combined; HR staff may shift from process execution to workforce strategy. PwC’s entry-level auditors are an example of training changes, with claimed benefits for client experience alongside continued emphasis on independence, quality and security. The source does not establish effects on law firms, ALSPs, legal departments or access to justice, and its enterprise claims should not be relabeled as legal-sector findings.
